Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a gastrointestinal motility disorder that results from the reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity resulting in symptoms or complications. The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx. GERD affects quality of life and may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. GERD is a clinical diagnosis and is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs). Long-term use of PPIs is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection.

Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) in children is very common and refers to the involuntary passage of gastric contents into the esophagus. This is often physiological and managed conservatively. In contrast, GER disease (GERD) is a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms, which may need medical management. Apart from abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, other factors that play a role in the pathogenesis of GERD include defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, as well as anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia. The clinical manifestations of GERD in young children are varied and nonspecific prompting the necessity for careful diagnostic evaluation. Management should be targeted to the underlying aetiopathogenesis and to limit complications of GERD. The following review focuses on up-to-date information regarding of the pathogenesis, diagnostic evaluation and management of GERD in children.

Symptoms potentially attributable to gastroesophageal reflux disease are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting. In this review, we discuss clinical approaches to the evaluation and management of these symptoms, including proton pump inhibitor trials as well as specific indications or clinical settings that warrant referral to Gastroenterology specialists.

data.narrative: GERD is a gastrointestinal motility disorder caused by reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity, producing symptoms or complications [18#0]. The typical symptoms are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx [18#1]. Symptoms potentially attributable to GERD are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting [20#2]. The condition is catalogued in MedGen as Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) [2] and is also indexed under the entity name Gastroesophageal Reflux [3]. Multiple PubMed records are titled Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [1][6][9][15]. GERD may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, which is a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma [18#3]. Long-term use of proton-pump inhibitors, the most effective treatment, is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection [18#4]. In children, GER is often physiological and managed conservatively, whereas GERD is a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms [19#5]. Factors contributing to pediatric GERD pathogenesis include abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, and anatomical defects such as hiatal hernia [19#6]. Clinical manifestations in young children are varied and nonspecific, necessitating careful diagnostic evaluation [19#7]. A review titled Gastroesophageal reflux disease in children: What's new right now? addresses current pathogenesis and management [12], and a clinical trial has studied the natural history of gastroesophageal reflux in children and adolescents [10]. Clinical approaches to evaluation and management include proton pump inhibitor trials as well as specific indications warranting referral to gastroenterology specialists [20#8]. Clinical trials have examined famotidine for non-erosive GERD [4], pantoprazole efficacy for acid reflux symptoms [7], on-demand treatment of reflux disease [13], and endoscopic fundoplication in a placebo-controlled study [16]. The associated publications include PMID 29132520 [5], PMID 33351044 [8], PMID 36170502 [11], PMID 37034973 [14], and PMID 37516506 [17].
